## This document is for practicing spline interpolation.

We need natural cubic splines that are monotonically increasing (`method = "hyman"`) and fit well with the model of the Lorenz curve.

I've manually calculated the $IP_k$ matrix for Vancouver's CMA, and will be using that data to test these methods.

```{r}
library(splines2)
```

```{r}
IPx <- sort(c(0.0,0.5,0.492629,0.902959715,0.992020086))
IPy <- sort(c(0.0,0.338737767,0.333333333,0.666666667,1))
```

```{r}
P <- splinefun(IPx, IPy, method = "hyman")
```

```{r}
P
```

```{r}
E = function(x){
  return((IPy[5]/IPx[5])*x)
}
```

We need to graph our interpolated function:

```{r}
x <- seq(IPx[1],IPx[5],length.out=1000)
y <- P(x)
Ey <- E(x)
```

```{r}
plot(IPx, IPy, pch = 19, main = "Lorenz Curve",
     xlab = "Population Share", ylab = "Income Share")
lines(x, y, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
lines(x, Ey, col = "green", lwd = 2)
```

Now we need to identify the Gini Coefficient.

```{r}
EP <- function(x){
  E(x)-P(x)
}
```

```{r}
areaA <- integrate(EP, IPx[1], IPx[5])
areaB <- integrate(E,IPx[1],IPx[5])
Gini <- areaA$value/areaB$value
```

We have our Gini coefficient! The Vancouver CMA has a Gini coefficient of `.326`.
